content.title: WHY YOUR 'HEALTHY' MEALS AREN'T ACTUALLY WORKING
facts: **Boiling vegetables** – This dumps most of the water-soluble vitamins straight into the drain; steaming or roasting keeps far more nutrients intact.
**Low-fat dressing** – Skipping oil on salads means your body can't absorb the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) locked in those veggies; add 1 tbsp olive oil.
**Overcooking chicken breast** – Cooking 'to be safe' well past 165°F just dries out the protein and doesn't add any extra safety.
**Rinsing canned beans quickly** – A 5-second rinse leaves behind sodium-heavy liquid; 30 seconds under running water cuts sodium significantly.
**Blending smoothies with juice** – Using juice instead of whole fruit or milk spikes the sugar content while stripping out fiber.
**Salting pasta water lightly** – Under-salting means the pasta itself stays bland, so people reach for extra sauce or cheese to compensate.
**Microwaving in the same container** – Reheating meals in thin plastic takeout containers can leach chemicals into food, especially with fatty sauces.
**Adding salt too early** – Salting meat right before it hits the pan pulls out moisture and prevents a proper sear, leading to tougher, drier results.

content.caption:
A few of these cooking habits quietly cancel out the effort you're putting into eating well. Take boiling vegetables — the moment you drop broccoli or spinach into hot water, vitamin C and B vitamins start dissolving out into the liquid, so unless you're drinking that water, you're pouring nutrients down the sink. Low-fat dressing is another sneaky one: vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, meaning your gut literally needs dietary fat present to absorb them, so a 'dry' salad can leave those nutrients passing right through you unused. And rinsing canned beans for just a couple seconds barely touches the starchy, sodium-packed liquid clinging to them — a real 30-second rinse under running water makes a noticeable difference. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so start with whichever one feels easiest to fix first.
